title: analysis and library costs
body: this legacy page is a short map to the foundation sequence: input size and operation counts (./input-size-and-operation-counts.md), asymptotic growth (./asymptotic-growth.md), cost models (./cost-models.md), loop invariants (./loop-invariants.md), array and python sequence costs (./arrays-and-python-costs.md), and recursion and recurrences (./recursion-and-recurrences.md). bitsandbytes/complexity.py — word ram model, o/θ/ω vocabulary, recursion limit, and the three recurrence shapes (merge divide, halving, linear decrement). bitsandbytes/library costs.py — why bfs uses deque , heapq.nsmallest , bisect.insort , and timsort; list.pop(0) costs o(n) element moves. industry a working engineer checks the language cost table before replacing a loop. python's time-complexity documentation lists list.pop(0) as o(n), because every later element moves, and says to use a collections.deque when both ends change. that deque documents approximately the same o(1) cost for appends and pops in either direction.

title: singly linked list
body: the idea a singly linked list stores each value in a node whose next reference points at the following node. the list keeps a head, a cached tail, and a size. the invariant is that following next from the head visits exactly size nodes and ends at the cached tail, whose next is empty. prepending changes the head in θ(1) time. appending with a cached tail changes the old tail's next and moves the tail pointer in θ(1) time. reading an index walks from the head, so it is θ(n). removing the tail is also θ(n), because the predecessor is not stored. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: list algorithms
body: this is the legacy overview and complexity index for the repository's list exercises. use the focused overviews for a first pass through fast/slow pointers (./fast-slow-pointer-patterns.md), reversal and relinking (./linked-list-reversal-and-relinking.md), merge and sort (./linked-list-merge-and-sort.md), and special input cases (./linked-list-special-cases.md). these modules only rewrite next on that shared list. any call that starts with require linear inherits that o(n) peak before the main loop. linked lists/reverse.py — iterative reversal is o(n) time and o(1) extra memory for the three pointers. the recursive form adds o(n) call-stack memory. linked lists/reverse in pairs.py — swap neighbours. o(n) time, o(1) extra memory for the loop. linked lists/reverse in blocks.py — reverse every block of k . each node is touched a constant number of times, so time is o(n), not o(n·k). linked lists/middle.py — fast and slow pointers; two different “middles” on even length. o(n) time. see the worked trace in the module docstring. linked lists/cycle.py — floyd’s algorithm finds a cycle entrance. o(n) time, o(1) extra memory for the walk itself. linked lists/remove cycle.py — clear the link that points back at the entrance. o(n) time, o(1) extra memory. linked lists/nth from end.py — a fixed gap of n nodes, then one walk together. o(length) time, o(1) extra memory for the two pointers. linked lists/duplicates.py — sorted duplicates are o(n) time and o(1) extra memory. unsorted duplicates use a set: expected o(n) time and o(n) extra memory. linked lists/rotate.py , partition.py , odd even.py , reorder.py — relinking only. o(n) time, o(1) extra memory for each loop. linked lists/palindrome.py — split at the left middle, reverse the second half, compare, restore. o(n) time, o(1) extra memory for the loop. linked lists/delete node.py — copy the successor forward. o(1). cannot delete the tail. linked lists/add numbers.py — least-significant digit at the head. o(n + m) time, o(1) scratch besides the result nodes. linked lists/merge sorted.py — merge two sorted chains by relinking. o(n + m) time, o(1) extra memory. linked lists/intersection.py — require linear on both lists, then equalize with cached lengths and walk in step. o(n + m) time; o(1) extra memory for the walk besides the guard peak. linked lists/sort list.py — bottom-up merge sort. o(n log n) time, o(1) extra memory besides nodes. stable. linked lists/split circular.py , modular nodes.py , reviewers.py — see each module’s cost section. modular node from end uses nth from end , so it is o(n) time and o(1) extra memory for the gap walk. industry a working engineer rewrites links when the records are already a chain. merging two sorted chains has a library twin: python's heapq.merge merges already-sorted inputs into one sorted output and does not pull every stream into memory at once. on these lists the same merge relinks the existing nodes.

title: doubly linked list and the lru cache
body: this legacy page is the implementation index. learn doubly linked-list operations (./doubly-linked-list-operations.md), then apply them to the lru cache (./lru-cache.md). bitsandbytes/doubly linked list.py — prev makes unlink and insert-beside-a-node o(1). reversal is o(n) time and o(1) extra memory. linked lists/random pointer.py — dictionary clone expected o(n) time and o(n) extra memory; interleaved clone o(n) time and o(1) scratch besides the copy. linked lists/lru cache.py — dictionary plus doubly linked list. get and put are expected o(1). resident memory is o(capacity). the hash table chapter explains why the dictionary lookup is expected o(1). industry a working engineer caches the most recent calls with functools.lru cache , which saves up to maxsize most recent calls. this course builds that policy as a hash table plus an order list: the dictionary finds the key, and the doubly linked list unlinks that node and moves it to the front without a scan. a singly linked order list would have to walk from the head to find the predecessor.

title: stacks
body: this legacy page is the implementation inventory. start with stack basics (./stack-basics.md), then choose monotonic stack patterns (./monotonic-stack-patterns.md) or stack parsing and expressions (./stack-parsing-and-expressions.md) for focused overviews. stacks/stack.py — bounded stack: capacity, decorator guards, amortized o(1) push , o(1) pop and peek . stacks/stack.py — stack(limit=none) is the unbounded stack used by algorithm lessons. the default limit stays 10. stacks/symbol balance.py — one pass. o(n) time, o(n) worst extra memory for openers. stacks/min stack.py — second stack of minima. push , pop , and minimum are o(1). stacks/next greater.py — monotonic stack. o(n) time, o(n) extra memory. stacks/stock span.py — same monotonic pattern. o(n) time. stacks/largest rectangle.py — histogram rectangle. o(n) time. stacks/infix postfix.py — shunting yard plus postfix evaluation. o(n) time. stacks/sort stack.py — one extra unbounded stack. worst case o(n²) time, o(n) extra memory. industry a working engineer uses a python list as a stack. the language tutorial says to add with append and to retrieve with pop() and no index, so the last item added is the first retrieved. the time-complexity documentation lists an end append and an end pop as amortized o(1).

title: sorting
body: this legacy page is the overview map. start with comparison sorts (./comparison-sorts.md), then follow merge sort (./merge-sort.md) and quicksort and partition (./quicksort-and-partition.md). for ranks and non-comparison methods, see the sorting extras overview (./sorting-extras.md). sorting/bubble sort.py — o(n²) worst and average, o(n) best on sorted input, o(1) extra memory. stable. sorting/selection sort.py — o(n²) for every input order. not stable. sorting/insertion sort.py — o(n²) worst and average, o(n) best. stable. sorting/merge sort.py — o(n log n) time, o(n) extra memory. stable. sorting/quick sort.py — lomuto partition: expected o(n log n), worst o(n²), including an all-equal list. quick sort three way handles duplicates in o(n) when every key matches. not stable. industry a working engineer calls list.sort . python's sorting howto names timsort and says it takes advantage of ordering already present in the data. list.sort is guaranteed stable, and the time-complexity documentation lists it as o(n log n) in the worst case. the quadratic sorts in this lesson are the hand derivations of a worse bound.

title: binary search
headings: find a value by ruling out half the list
the idea: keep only possible answers
why the search takes logarithmic time
body: find a value by ruling out half the list by the end of this lesson, you can trace binary search, explain why each discarded index cannot contain the answer, handle a missing value and duplicate values, and distinguish the cost of searching from the cost of inserting. before you start: you should be comfortable reading a python list, comparing values, and following while loops. no prior search-algorithm knowledge is required. the page states how long the explanation and practice take. start with a prediction the numbers below are already sorted. you want to find 7 : if you inspect the middle value first, which indexes can you rule out after seeing that it is 5 ? pause on your prediction, then use the trace controls below to check it and step through the search. the idea: keep only possible answers binary search needs values in sorted order and a way to access the middle position directly. keep two indexes, left and right , for the still-possible range. at each step: 1. choose the middle index of that range. 2. if its value is too small, keep only the part to its right. 3. if its value is too large, keep only the part to its left. 4. if neither comparison is true, the value matches. the important invariant is: if the target is in the sequence, it is somewhere in the current range . each comparison preserves that statement while making the range smaller. trace the search this implementation uses a closed, or inclusive, range: both left and right are possible indexes. 1. start: left = 0 , right = 4 . the whole list, indexes 0 through 4, is possible. 2. first comparison: middle = 2 , whose value is 5. since 7 5 , set left = middle + 1 . indexes 3 through 4 remain possible. 3. second comparison: middle = 3 , whose value is 7. the target is found at index 3. when the target is smaller than the middle value, set right = middle - 1 instead. the middle index itself is excluded because its value has already been shown to be too large. read the implementation this is the repository’s actual inclusive-range binary search function. the site inserts the marked function directly from bitsandbytes/search/binary search.py during its build, so the displayed code follows the source implementation. source-excerpt:binary-search the loop condition is left <= right because a range containing exactly one index is still worth checking. if the range becomes empty ( left right ), the target was not present, so the function returns -1 . the code uses two < comparisons instead of requiring values to support <= . if neither value is less than the other, they are equivalent for this search order and the function returns that index. the input must be non-decreasing under < . a different convention: half-open ranges the repository’s lower bound and upper bound functions use a half-open range, left, right) : include the left endpoint but exclude the right endpoint. they start with right = len(values) , so the range can represent the insertion point just after the last item. their loop condition is left < right ; when the indexes meet, that index is the answer. these bounds are useful, but mixing their loop condition or endpoint updates with the inclusive implementation above causes off-by-one errors. missing values, duplicates and boundaries - missing value: for 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 , searching for 6 eventually makes the range empty and returns -1 . - one item: 8 searching for 8 checks index 0 once. searching for 2 checks it once and returns -1 . - empty input: with , right starts at -1 ; 0 <= -1 is false, so the result is -1 without indexing the list. - duplicates: binary search may return any matching index. use bounds when you need the full matching interval. in 1, 2, 2, 2, 3 , lower bound(..., 2) is 1 and upper bound(..., 2) is 4. the number of matches is 4 - 1 = 3 . the corresponding cases are covered by the repository’s binary-search tests (https://github.com/ishitvagoel/bitsandbytes/blob/master/tests/test search and sort extras.py). why the search takes logarithmic time suppose there are n candidates. after one comparison there are at most n/2 ; after two, at most n/4 . after k comparisons, at most n / 2^k remain. the range is empty or has one candidate once 2^k is at least n , which takes about log₂(n) comparisons. therefore search takes o(log n) time and stores only a few indexes, so it uses o(1) extra space. this analysis assumes the sequence is already sorted, comparisons take constant time, and indexing reaches a middle element in constant time, as it does for a python list. sorting first has its own cost and is not included. binary search on a linked list does not get the same time bound because reaching each middle position requires traversal. finding an insertion point is also logarithmic with python’s bisect (https://docs.python.org/3/library/bisect.html) module. inserting into the middle of a python list is still o(n) in the worst case: later elements need to shift to make room. thus bisect.insort is o(n) overall even though its search step is o(log n). practice: predict, debug and transfer use the checkpoint cards below to make a prediction, diagnose a non-shrinking range, transfer the bounds idea to duplicates, and explain why searching for an insertion point does not make list insertion logarithmic. each response includes feedback explaining the reasoning. next step try tracing a target that is absent and explain why every discarded index is impossible. then continue to binary search on an answer (./binary-search-on-answer.md) to apply the shrinking-range idea to a monotone yes/no condition, followed by sorting (./05-sorting.md).

title: queues and deque
body: this legacy page is the implementation inventory. learn fifo and double-ended operations in queue and deque operations (./queue-and-deque-operations.md), then compare resizing in dynamic-array growth (./dynamic-array-growth.md). queues/linked queue.py — fifo with a doubly linked list. enqueue and dequeue are o(1). queues/circular queue.py — fixed-capacity ring buffer with an explicit size counter. enqueue and dequeue are o(1). linear/dynamic array.py — geometric doubling; n appends copy o(n) elements in total. deques/linked deque.py — o(1) at both ends on a doubly linked list; middle insert is o(n). industry a working engineer implements a queue with collections.deque . the python tutorial says a list is a poor queue, because an insert or pop at the beginning shifts every other element, and that collections.deque has fast appends and pops at both ends. the deque documentation states approximately the same o(1) performance in either direction, which is why list.pop(0) is the operation to avoid.

title: heaps
body: this legacy page is the implementation index. review the heap invariant and heapsort (./heap-operations.md), then see priority queues (./priority-queues.md) for indexed updates. heaps/heapsort.py — heapify is o(n); heapsort is o(n log n) time and o(1) extra memory. not stable. heaps/priority queue.py — min-heap with decrease key through an index map. push, pop, and decrease-key are o(log n). industry a working engineer uses heapq as a priority queue. python documents a min-heap whose smallest item is always heap 0 , with heapify in linear time. removing that root and restoring the heap is logarithmic, and repeating the removal sorts in o(n log n). the same page notes that this heapsort is not stable, which is also true of heapsort here.

title: hash table
body: this legacy page is the implementation index. compare separate chaining (./hash-chaining.md) with linear probing (./hash-linear-probing.md) to see two ways to resolve collisions. hash tables/chaining.py — separate chaining. expected o(1) lookup and insert; rehash is o(n) but amortized. hash tables/linear probing.py — open addressing with tombstones. degenerate chain length explains a one-bucket table. industry a working engineer uses a dict for lookup by key. python's time-complexity documentation lists average-case get, set, and delete as o(1), and o(n) when every key hashes to the same bucket. separate chaining is one bucket's list; that worst case is why a degenerate hash is part of this lesson.

title: binary search tree
body: this legacy page is the implementation index. start with bst operations (./binary-search-tree-operations.md), then study traversals (./tree-traversals.md) and balanced search trees (./balanced-search-trees.md). trees/bst.py — insert, search, delete, and in-order walk. o(h) per operation for height h. trees/traversals.py — preorder, postorder, and level order in o(n) time. trees/llrb.py — left-leaning red-black tree with rank and select in o(log n). industry a working engineer reaches for a b-tree when keys must answer equality and range comparisons. postgresql's index documentation says create index builds a b-tree by default, and that a b-tree handles < , <= , = , = , and . the binary search tree in this lesson is that comparison walk in memory. sorted insertion makes its height linear, which is why the left-leaning red-black tree keeps the height logarithmic.

title: union-find
body: the idea a disjoint-set forest tracks which items are in the same set. each item stores a parent. the root is the item whose parent is itself, and it names the set. find walks parents to the root. union merges two sets by pointing one root at the other. without heuristics, union(0, 1) sets parent 1 = 0, and union(1, 2) finds that 1's root is already 0 and sets parent 2 = 0. find(2) and find(0) then return the same root. the library's disjointset(3, use heuristics=false) does this. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: sorting extras
body: this legacy page is the implementation map. use the focused pages for counting and radix sorts (./noncomparison-sorts.md), order-statistic selection (./order-statistic-selection.md), binary search on a feasible answer (./binary-search-on-answer.md), and inversion counting (./inversion-counting.md). sorting/selection and radix.py — comparison lower bound, counting and lsd radix sorts, quickselect, binary search on the answer, inversion count. industry a working engineer does not sort the whole input when only the smallest few values are required. python's sorting howto points at heapq.nsmallest for that job: one pass that keeps only the requested number of elements. digit keys are the other case in this lesson, counting sort and lsd radix, because a comparison lower bound does not apply to them.

title: graphs
body: graphs/adjacency list.py — adjacency lists. dfs and bfs are o(v + e). the teaching dijkstra distances scans all unsettled vertices each step, so o(v²) time on dense graphs. focused lessons - graph representations (./53-graph-representations.md) - graph traversals (./54-graph-traversals.md) - directed acyclic graphs and topological order (./55-topological-order.md) - shortest paths (./56-shortest-paths.md) - minimum spanning trees (./57-minimum-spanning-trees.md) graphs/algorithms.py — bfs distances, topological sort, cycle detection, kosaraju sccs, bellman-ford, heap dijkstra, kruskal, prim, 0-1 bfs, floyd-warshall, bipartite test. industry a working engineer stores a sparse graph as adjacency lists and searches with the structure the weights require. unweighted breadth-first search uses collections.deque , which python documents with approximately o(1) appends and pops at either end. non-negative weights use heapq , the min-heap whose smallest item is the root. the adjacency-list scan is the dijkstra that heap replaces.

title: dynamic programming
body: the idea dynamic programming applies when a problem repeats smaller versions of itself and you can order those versions. so each one is ready before you need it. the fibonacci recurrence f(n) = f(n - 1) + f(n - 2), with f(0) = 0 and f(1) = 1, is the smallest example. a naive recursion recomputes f(3) many times. a bottom-up table fills each index once. the library function fibonacci modulo keeps only the last two values and returns f(n) mod m. for n = 6 and m = 1000 the result is 8. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: greedy algorithms
body: greedy/classic.py — interval scheduling, fractional knapsack, huffman codes. industry a working engineer uses a min-heap when the greedy choice is the lightest remaining weight. huffman coding in this module repeatedly takes the two lightest weights with heapq.heappop . python documents a min-heap whose smallest item is heap 0 , and heappop returns that item.

title: backtracking and array patterns
body: backtracking/search.py — permutations, combinations, subsets, n-queens count. focused lessons - two-pointer patterns (./58-two-pointers.md) - sliding windows (./59-sliding-window.md) - prefix sums (./60-prefix-sums.md) - backtracking search (./61-backtracking.md) - greedy methods (./62-greedy-methods.md) - dynamic programming state and transitions (./63-dp-state-and-transition.md) patterns/arrays.py — two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, monotonic-queue window maximum. industry a working engineer writes a backtracking search when a partial choice can be rejected, and a forward scan when the constraint is a window. the sliding-window maximum in this lesson keeps candidate indexes in a collections.deque . python documents approximately o(1) appends and pops at either end, so each index can enter the deque and leave it once.

title: strings
body: strings/algorithms.py — trie, kmp, rabin-karp, inverted index, run-length encoding, suffix array with lcp. focused lessons - string search algorithms (./64-string-search.md) - tries and text indexes (./65-tries-and-text-indexes.md) industry a working engineer answers which documents contain a term with an inverted index. postgresql documents gin indexes as inverted indexes: a separate entry for each component value, so a query can test whether that value is present. invertedindex in this module is that map from a term to its posting list.

title: range queries and approximate structures
body: range queries/structures.py — fenwick tree, lazy segment tree, sparse table for rmq. focused lessons - range-query structures (./66-range-query-structures.md) - approximate membership structures (./67-approximate-membership.md) approximate/structures.py — bloom filter, skip list, persistent stack frames. industry a working engineer uses a bloom filter when a definite miss is enough to skip a lookup. redis documents bf.add to add an item and bf.exists to test one: a hit means the item was probably added, and a miss means it was definitely not. a fenwick tree or a segment tree is the structure in this lesson when the answer has to be an exact prefix or an exact range.

title: storage and locality
body: storage/engines.py — in-memory b-tree, write-ahead log, toy lsm with bloom-filtered runs, scan benchmark, brute-force nearest neighbor. focused lesson - storage engines and locality (./68-storage-engines-and-locality.md) industry a working engineer stores ordered keys in a b-tree, or buffers writes and flushes sorted runs. postgresql's documentation makes the b-tree the default create index for equality and range queries. rocksdb's overview describes the write path this module models: new writes go into a memtable and optionally a write-ahead log, a full memtable is flushed to a sorted sst file, and compaction merges files into sorted runs.

title: limits and approximation
body: limits/approximation.py — 2-approximation vertex cover. focused lesson - approximation guarantees (./69-approximation-guarantees.md) industry a working engineer distinguishes a proven lower bound from an unresolved complexity assumption. general minimum vertex cover is np-hard; no exact polynomial-time algorithm is known. for a simple approximation, repeatedly choose an uncovered edge and add its endpoints. the chosen edges are pairwise vertex-disjoint, giving a 2-approximation.

title: appendix: python tools
body: these are not the next data-structure lesson after graphs. they stay in the repo as small python examples. decorators/permission.py — wrapper is o(1) plus the wrapped call. decorators/access control.py — expected o(1) permission lookup, then the action. tools/print directory.py — os.walk is o(entries). print directory paths.py still runs the directory walk. industry a working engineer wraps a function instead of copying its body. functools.wraps , applied to the confirmation wrapper, copies the wrapped callable's metadata onto the wrapper so the visible name stays the original function's name. walking a directory tree is os.walk , which yields each directory top-down or bottom-up.

title: fast and slow pointers
body: the idea a linked list has no index, so two pointers replace a length calculation. the fast pointer moves two links for every one link the slow pointer moves. when fast falls off a linear list, slow is at a middle node. middle node on 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 returns the node holding 3. on an even list the same function returns the second of the two middles. middle node on 1, 2, 3, 4 returns 3. end of first half stops one step sooner and returns 2, the left middle. palindrome and reorder split there. if the links form a cycle, fast gains one node per iteration and meets slow inside the cycle. reset one pointer to the head and walk both one step at a time. they meet at the entrance. on 1 through 5 with the tail linked to 3, find cycle start returns index 3. a fixed gap finds a node from the end. move a lead pointer k links ahead, then move both pointers together. the gap stays k. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: linked-list reversal and relinking
body: the idea reversal rearranges a chain by changing next references, not by copying values. before you overwrite a link, save the node that follows it. otherwise the unvisited suffix becomes unreachable. reverse iterative keeps three names. previous is the reversed prefix. current is the node being flipped. upcoming is the saved suffix. the library starts previous empty and current at the head. each step saves current.next, points current.next at previous, then advances both moving names. when current is empty, previous is the new head. on 1, 2, 3 the result is 3, 2, 1. pair and block reversal reuse the same invariant. they must also reconnect the previous block to the new head of the current block, and connect that block's tail to the untouched suffix. rotation finds a new tail, makes the chain temporarily circular, then cuts it. partition and odd-even grouping keep separate tails, then join the chains. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: linked-list merge and sort
body: the idea when two chains are sorted, compare only their current heads. take the smaller head, append it to the result, and advance that input. when one input is empty, attach the other suffix. it is already in order. merge sorted of 1, 4 and 2, 3 returns 1, 2, 3, 4. ties use a strict less-than against the second list, so an equal key from the first list stays in front. the nodes are relinked, not copied into a second array of values. both inputs are left empty because their nodes now belong to the result. merging a list with itself is rejected, because that would build a cycle. bottom-up merge sort repeats this combine on adjacent runs of width 1, then 2, then 4. a linked list has no random-access middle, so this width schedule fits it better than a top-down split that indexes the midpoint. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: special linked-list cases
body: the idea some linked-list routines are valid only under a contract that is easy to miss. values may be sorted. digits may be stored least-significant digit first. a circular list may have a distinguished head. the function may receive one node and not the list head. nth from end makes its contract explicit. n is 1-based, and 1 means the tail. on 1, 2, 3, 4, nth from end with n equal to 2 returns the node holding 3. the leader walks n steps first. then the leader and the trailer walk together. when the leader falls off, the trailer is the requested node. removing adjacent duplicates in a sorted list needs only a neighbor comparison. the sorted precondition is what makes that enough. an unsorted list needs a set of seen values, which changes the memory. deleting a node without the list head can copy the successor and bypass it. that trick cannot remove the tail, because there is no successor to copy. adding numbers stored least-significant digit first can walk both heads and carry one digit. splitting a circular list must restore two cycles and handle an odd count and an even count. reviewerslist is a circular list with its own node type. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: input size and operation counts
body: the idea name the input size before you count work. for one list, n is the number of items. for a graph, say v vertices and e edges instead of one n. an operation is one comparison, one link follow, or one arithmetic step that does not itself hide a loop. a single loop from 0 to n - 1 does n iterations. a nested loop that compares every index with every later index does (n - 1) + (n - 2) + ... + 1 checks. that sum is n(n - 1) / 2. dropping the constant 1/2 and the lower term is a later step. this lesson keeps the exact count so the next lesson has something real to bound. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: asymptotic growth
body: the idea an exact count such as 3n + 20 is useful, and it is also more precise than the decision you usually need. big o, θ, and ω compare growth. o(f) says the work is at most a constant times f for large n. ω(f) says it is at least a constant times f. θ(f) says both, so f is a tight description. 3n + 20 is θ(n) because (3n + 20) / n approaches 3. it is also o(n²), since a looser upper bound is still true, but θ(n²) is false. when you write a cost in this guide, prefer the tight bound and say so. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: cost models and assumptions
body: the idea a complexity claim is true only inside a stated model. the word-ram model charges one step for a comparison, a pointer write, or word-sized arithmetic. that model fits a list of machine words. it is the wrong model when one named step hides a loop. a python list is a dynamic array of references. reading an index is one address calculation. list.pop(0) moves every later reference one slot toward index 0. list pop front cost demo(3) returns 2. those two writes are the items that remain after the front item leaves. a linked list has no constant-time middle. binary search stays logarithmic only when each index is constant time. count the container operation the code actually performs. state a key-size assumption before you call hashing constant time. count the recursion stack apart from the loop variables. the point of this lesson is to separate algorithm steps from python container costs. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: loop invariants
body: the idea a loop invariant is a statement that is true before the loop and after every iteration. it is the reason the loop's final state means what you think it means. three checks make the argument. initialization says the statement holds before the first iteration. preservation says one iteration that starts from a true statement ends with the statement still true. termination says the loop stops, and the invariant plus the exit condition is the result you wanted. insertion sort's invariant is that the prefix values 0:i is sorted at the start of the outer step that inserts values i . a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: arrays and python sequence costs
body: the idea a python list is a dynamic array of references. indexing list i is θ(1) because the address is base + i times the reference size. append and pop() at the end are cheap on average, which the next lesson counts. insert(0, x) and pop(0) move every later reference, so one call is θ(n). a collections.deque stores blocks that can grow at either end, so append and popleft are θ(1). use a list when you need random access. use a deque when both ends change and you do not need list i in the inner loop. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: recursion and recurrences
body: the idea a recurrence describes a function that calls itself. the one you will meet in merge sort is t(n) = 2 t(n/2) + θ(n), with t(1) = θ(1). the 2 t(n/2) is the two recursive calls. the θ(n) is the work to merge the halves. unrolling the recurrence shows log2(n) levels, because the input size halves each time. θ(n) work on every level, because the pieces at one level add up to n. the product is θ(n log n). the call stack on one path is θ(log n) frames deep. that is extra memory even when each frame stores only a few indexes. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: stack basics
body: the idea a stack is a last-in, first-out sequence. push adds an item at the top. pop removes that same item. the size invariant is 0 ≤ size ≤ limit for a bounded stack, and size changes by exactly 1 on every successful push or pop. the teaching stack in this repository stores items in a python list and rejects a push that would pass the limit. after push 1, push 2, push 3, the first pop returns 3 and the second returns 2. that order is the definition, not an accident of the example. a python list is the same stack when you append to push and call pop with no argument. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: monotonic stack patterns
body: the idea a monotonic stack stores indexes that are still waiting for an answer. next greater on 2, 1, 2, 4, 3 returns 4, 2, 4, none, and none. the stack holds indexes. when a larger value arrives, every index it beats is popped and that value is written as the answer. indexes that remain at the end have no strictly greater value on their right. stock spans uses the same waiting stack. on prices 100, 80, 60, 70, 60, 75, 85 the span at the 75 is 4, because the walk stops at a strictly higher price. largest rectangle asks for the nearest shorter bar on each side. the area is height times the gap between those bars. on 2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3 the largest area is 10. min stack keeps the current minimum beside the values. after pushing 3, then 1, then 2, the minimum is 1, and it is still 1 after 2 is popped. sort stack uses a second stack so each moved value lands in order. the shared rule is that a value leaves the stack only when a later value resolves it. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: stack parsing and expressions
body: the idea a bracket stack stores unmatched opening marks. symbols are balanced pushes each opener and pops when a closer arrives. the closer must match the current top. other characters are ignored, so a formula and a bare bracket string share one checker. ( ) is balanced. ( ) is not, because the closer for the square bracket arrives while the parenthesis is still on top. an empty string is balanced. a leftover opener is not. operator precedence uses a second stack. infix to postfix turns 2+3 4 into the tokens 2, 3, 4, , +. multiplication leaves the operator stack before addition because it binds more tightly. evaluate infix of that expression returns 14. the value stack applies an operator only when both of its operands are already values. that is why postfix does not need parentheses. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: queue and deque operations
body: the idea a queue is first-in, first-out. enqueue adds at the back and dequeue removes from the front. the linked queue in this repository uses a doubly linked list with a cached tail, so both ends are θ(1). a ring buffer stores the same order in an array with a head index and a tail index. a deque allows add and remove at both ends. the order promise is the part to learn first. after enqueue a, b, c, two dequeues return a and then b. a python list can act as a stack with append and pop at the end, and that is a different order from this queue. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: dynamic-array growth
body: the idea a dynamic array stores items in a contiguous block and remembers a length and a capacity. append writes into the next free slot when length < capacity. when the block is full, the array allocates a new block with twice the capacity, copies the old references, and then writes the new item. the example starts at capacity 1. appending a, b, and c copies 0, then 1, then 2 references. the library's dynamicarray.capacity after those three appends is 4, and the stored items are a, b, c. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: comparison sorts
body: the idea a comparison sort decides order only by asking whether one key is less than another. insertion sort keeps a sorted prefix and inserts the next key into it. selection sort grows a sorted prefix by swapping the minimum of the suffix into place. bubble sort walks neighbors and swaps inversions. all three are θ(n²) in the worst case. they differ in the best case, in stability, and in how many writes they perform. insertion sort on a sorted list is θ(n) because each new key is already in place. the library function insertion sort( 3, 1, 2 ) returns 1, 2, 3 . python's list.sort uses timsort, a stable merge sort. it is o(n log n) and it keeps runs that are already ordered. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: merge sort
body: the idea merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half, and merges the two sorted runs. the midpoint is len(values) // 2, integer division, so the halves differ by at most one item. the merge walks the two fronts and appends the smaller one. when the keys are equal it appends the left front, so equal keys keep the order they had in the input. the library merge sort( 3, 1, 4, 2 ) returns 1, 2, 3, 4 and does not modify the input list. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: quicksort and partition
body: the idea quicksort picks a pivot, partitions the range so every value before the pivot is ≤ the pivot. every value after it is the pivot, and then sorts the two sides. the library's partition swaps the chosen pivot to the end and scans once. boundary is the next slot that should receive a value ≤ pivot. for pivot 2 at the end of 3, 1, 4, 2 , the scan swaps 1 to index 0. then swaps 2 into index 1, leaving 1, 2, 4, 3 . the recursive calls sort the two sides. quick sort on this input returns 1, 2, 3, 4 . the pivot index itself is random unless you pass a random instance. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: counting and radix sorts
body: the idea comparison sorts need a logarithmic number of comparisons per item in the worst case when they learn order only by comparing keys. counting sort skips comparisons when the keys are integers in a known range. counting sort of 3, 1, 2, 1 with maximum 3 returns 1, 1, 2, 3. it counts how many keys have each value, then writes them into those slots. equal keys keep their order if the write walks the input from left to right into the next free slot of that count. that stability is what a radix sort needs. lsd radix sort of 170, 45, 75, 90, 802, 24, 2, 66 returns 2, 24, 45, 66, 75, 90, 170, 802. each pass sorts by one digit, starting at the least significant digit, and the next pass must not scramble the order the previous pass built. the digit alphabet is the base, here 10. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: order-statistic selection
body: the idea an order statistic is the k-th smallest key, counting from zero. sorting would find it, and would also order every other key. quickselect stops when the pivot lands on k. on a copy of 3, 1, 4, 2, quickselect with k = 0 returns 1. the same input with k = 2 returns 3, the third smallest key in 1, 2, 3, 4. the library partition always uses the rightmost value as the pivot. it walks the range once, swaps smaller keys toward the left boundary, and writes the pivot into the boundary. if that index is k, the pivot is the answer. if k is smaller, the search continues on the left side only. if k is larger, it continues on the right side only. the discarded side is not sorted. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: binary search on a feasible answer
headings: find a boundary by asking a yes-or-no question
keep the first feasible rate in range
body: find a boundary by asking a yes-or-no question sometimes the answer is not an item in a sorted list. instead, you can test a candidate answer: “if the machine works at this rate, can it finish on time?” when those yes/no results change only once across an ordered range, binary search can locate the boundary. by the end of this lesson, you can state the monotonicity condition, trace a smallest-feasible search, and multiply the number of feasibility checks by the cost of one check. before you start: you should be able to follow the left , right and midpoint updates in binary search (./06-binary-search.md). allow about 15 minutes to work through the trace and checks. make the decision monotone suppose four piles contain 3, 6, 7, 11 items. a machine processes one pile at a time and works at a fixed positive rate for one hour on each pile. what is the smallest integer rate that finishes in at most eight hours? for a candidate rate r , the hours needed for a pile of size p are ceil(p / r) . add those hours over all piles. a rate is feasible if the total is at most eight. if a rate is feasible, every faster rate is also feasible. if a rate is too slow, every slower rate is also infeasible. the answers therefore look like false, false, ..., true, true ; finding the first true is a boundary search. this one-change pattern is the required monotonicity condition . if feasible and infeasible candidates alternate, rejecting half the range is not justified: the discarded half could still contain the first feasible answer. keep the first feasible rate in range let low be the smallest rate still possible and high a rate already known to be feasible. maintain the invariant: the smallest feasible rate is somewhere in the inclusive interval low, high , and high is feasible . the largest pile size is a feasible upper bound when the number of available hours is at least the number of piles: at that rate every pile takes one hour. if fewer hours than piles are available, no rate can finish the work under these rules. at the midpoint, a feasible rate may be the answer, so keep it by setting high = middle . an infeasible midpoint and every slower rate are too small, so set low = middle + 1 . both updates preserve the invariant and make the interval smaller. | low | high | middle | hours at middle | decision | remaining interval | |

title: inversion counting
body: the idea an inversion is a pair of indexes i < j whose values are out of order, value i greater than value j. inversion count on 3, 1, 4, 2 returns 3. the pairs are 3 before 1, 3 before 2, and 4 before 2. a sorted array has zero inversions. a reversed array has one inversion per pair. the library counts them while it merges, the same split merge sort uses. inside one sorted run there are no new inversions. every inversion that still matters has one endpoint in the left run and one in the right run. when the merge takes from the right run while the left run still has a smaller-index key waiting. that left key and every key still in the left run form inversions with the key just taken. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: hash tables with chaining
body: the idea separate chaining stores a list of key-value pairs in each bucket. the hash of the key picks the bucket. insert appends a pair, or replaces the value if the key is already in that list. lookup scans the list and compares keys. with a 4-bucket table, hash(0) % 4 and hash(4) % 4 are both 0, so inserting 0. then 4 places both pairs in one chain. a later lookup of 0 walks that chain and returns 1. the library chaininghashtable does this, and len stays 2 because the keys differ. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: hash tables with linear probing
body: the idea linear probing stores one key in each slot of an array. the hash picks a start slot. if that slot is occupied by a different key, the insert tries the next slot, then the next, wrapping at the end of the array. a linearprobinghashtable with capacity 4 stores key 0 in slot 0. key 4 has the same start slot, finds it full, and takes slot 1. lookup of 4 repeats that probe and returns 2. deleting 0 does not write an empty slot. it writes a tombstone. lookup of 4 must skip the tombstone and continue, otherwise it would stop and miss a key that sits further along the same probe. an empty slot still means the key is absent. the table rehashes when the number of live keys would reach half the capacity, which keeps clusters shorter. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: binary search tree operations
body: the idea a binary search tree node holds a key, a left child, and a right child. every key in the left subtree is < the node's key, and every key in the right subtree is it. insert walks that rule until it finds an empty child, then hangs the new key there. inserting 4, 2, 6, 1 puts 4 at the root, 2 on its left, 6 on its right, and 1 on the left of 2. the library's inorder walk visits left, node, right, so it returns 1, 2, 4, 6 . a duplicate key is ignored. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: tree traversals
body: the idea a traversal is a rule for the order in which you visit nodes. the same tree produces different sequences under different rules. build the binary search tree by inserting 4, then 2, then 6, then 1. preorder visits a node before either child and returns 4, 2, 1, 6. postorder visits both children before the node and returns 1, 2, 6, 4. the inorder walk, left then node then right, returns 1, 2, 4, 6. which is the sorted order only because the tree is a search tree. level order uses a queue. it returns 4, 2, 6, 1. the root leaves first. its children are enqueued left then right, so 2 is ahead of 6, and 1 waits behind them. depth-first walks use a stack, or the call stack. breadth-first walks use a queue. the container is the difference. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: balanced search trees
body: the idea a plain binary search tree becomes a chain when keys arrive in sorted order. every operation then walks n nodes. a balanced tree keeps the height logarithmic by local rotations. the library's left-leaning red-black tree encodes a 2-3 tree. a red link to a left child means two keys share a node. right-leaning red links are rotated away. insert 1, then 2, then 3. the inorder walk is 1, 2, 3, so the search-tree order survives. the root key is 2, not 3, so the tree did not become a chain. select(1) returns 2, the second smallest key. rank(2) returns 1, the number of keys strictly smaller than 2. those order statistics come from subtree sizes stored on the nodes. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: heap operations
body: the idea a complete tree fills every level except possibly the last, and that last level fills from the left. a binary heap stores a complete tree in an array. python's heapq is this structure as a min-heap. heappop returns the smallest item. for a max-heap, every parent is ≥ its children, so the largest key is at index 0. the children of index i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. heapify starts at the last parent and sifts that item down until the invariant holds. on 3, 1, 4, 2 the last parent is index 1. sifting swaps 1 with 2, leaving 3, 2, 4, 1 . sifting the root then swaps 3 with 4, leaving 4, 2, 3, 1 . heapsort extracts the root until the array is sorted. the library returns 1, 2, 3, 4 . a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: priority queues
body: the idea a priority queue returns the best priority, not the oldest item and not the newest item. the library's priorityqueue is a binary min-heap. push(5, a), push(3, b), and push(4, c) leave 3 at the root. the first pop returns the pair 3, b. later pops return 4, c and then 5, a. each push returns a token. decrease key uses that token to find the heap index without scanning. the heap stores priority, token, and item. the token breaks ties so two equal priorities stay distinct. this is the structure dijkstra and prim need when they repeatedly ask for the next smallest tentative weight. sorting the whole set once is cheaper when you need every item in order and you will not insert anything in between. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: doubly linked-list operations
body: the idea a doubly linked node stores prev and next. if you already hold the node, you do not walk from the head to find its neighbors. remove node on the node for a, in a list that also holds b, returns a and leaves b. the unlink follows prev and next and rewires those neighbors to each other. insert after splices a new node between a known node and that node's next. both directions must be written. a missing reverse link makes a forward walk and a backward walk disagree. finding a node by value is still linear, unless another structure stores the node. sentinels are one way to make every real node have neighbors, including the empty list. this list keeps a head and a tail instead, and the endpoint cases update those caches. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: lru cache
body: the idea an lru cache of capacity k keeps the k most recently used keys. the library uses two structures. a dictionary maps a key to the node that holds it. a doubly linked list orders those nodes by use. the head side is the most recent key and the tail side is the least recent. get moves a hit to the front. put of an existing key updates the value and moves that node to the front. put of a new key evicts the tail when the cache is already full, then inserts the new key at the front. start with capacity 2. put a, put b, get a, put c. b was used before a, so b is the tail and c evicts it. get b then returns none. get a returns 1 and get c returns 3. a missing get returns none rather than raising. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: graph representations
body: the idea a graph can be stored as an adjacency list or as a matrix. the library graph is a dictionary from each vertex to a list of neighbor and weight pairs. add a to b, a to c, and b to d. the graph has 4 vertices and 3 outgoing pairs. a matrix for the same vertices has 16 cells, one for every ordered pair, almost all of them empty. the list stores only the edges you added. a sparse graph is one where the edge count is much smaller than the square of the vertex count. breadth-first search on that shape should use a queue with constant-time ends. python's collections.deque is the usual choice. the library's own breadth-first search uses its linked queue for the same reason. scanning a matrix row to find neighbors costs a full vertex scan even when a vertex has one edge. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: graph traversals
body: the idea breadth-first search uses a queue. depth-first search uses a stack, or the call stack. both mark a vertex when they first discover it so an edge back to a visited vertex does not enqueue it again. on the directed graph a→b, a→c, b→d, breadth-first order from a is a, b, c, d. b and c are both neighbors of a, and b is enqueued first because it is the first edge. d is discovered from b, so it waits behind c. the library function breadth first order returns that list. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: directed acyclic graphs and topological order
body: the idea a topological order is a list of the vertices of a directed graph such that every edge points forward in the list. topological order on edges a to b, a to c, b to d, and c to d returns a, b, c, d. kahn's algorithm computes an indegree for each vertex. it starts a queue with every vertex whose indegree is zero. a is the only such vertex here. when a vertex leaves the queue, each outgoing edge reduces a neighbor's indegree. a neighbor enters the queue when its indegree hits zero. b and c both become ready after a, and d waits until both of its incoming edges have been counted. has directed cycle on this graph is false. on a two-cycle from a to b and back, it is true, and topological order raises valueerror. because the queue runs dry before every vertex has been emitted. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: shortest paths
body: the idea the shortest-path algorithm you want depends on the weights. unweighted edges can use breadth-first search, because the fewest edges is the shortest path. non-negative weights can use dijkstra. negative weights need bellman-ford, which also reports a negative cycle if you ask it to keep relaxing. on edges a to b weight 1, a to c weight 4, and b to c weight 2. dijkstra distances heap from a gives c the distance 3. the direct edge is not the best path. relaxation is the step that discovers this. when b's distance is final, the edge b to c offers 1 + 2, which beats 4. bellman ford distances on a to b weight 1 and b to c weight -2 gives c the distance -1. dijkstra is not the right call once a weight can be negative. zero one bfs distances on a path of two weight-1 edges gives c the distance 2. floyd warshall on that path also gives a to c the distance 2, and it fills every pair. is bipartite is true on the path and false on a directed triangle, which is an odd cycle. kosaraju strongly connected components on that triangle returns one component containing a, c, and b. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: minimum spanning trees
body: the idea a minimum spanning tree connects every vertex of an undirected weighted graph and has the smallest total edge weight. prim and kruskal both return 3 on the triangle a-b weight 1, b-c weight 2, and a-c weight 4. kruskal sorts edges by weight and adds an edge when its ends lie in different components. the weight-4 edge finds a and c already connected through b, so the union-find cycle check rejects it. prim grows one tree from a. it adds the cheapest edge that leaves the visited set. that is a-b, then b-c. the edge back to a is ignored because a is already visited. the two algorithms can pick different edges when weights tie. they do not pick different totals on this graph. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: two-pointer patterns
body: the idea two pointers scan a sorted array from the ends, or scan a sequence with a start and an end that only move forward. two sum sorted on 1, 2, 4, 7 with target 6 returns indexes 1 and 2, the positions of 2 and 4. the left index starts at 0 and the right index starts at the last item. if the sum is too small, the left index moves right, because every value further left is even smaller. if the sum is too large, the right index moves left. each move throws away a value that cannot be part of any remaining pair. the loop stops when the indexes meet. a pair of nested loops would also find the pair, and would check every combination. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: sliding windows
body: the idea a sliding window is a contiguous slice that moves across the input. you keep a fact about the slice and update it when the slice grows or shrinks, instead of recomputing from scratch. sliding window maximum on 1, 3, 2, 5 with window 2 returns 3, 3, 5. a deque stores indexes of candidates. the front is the index of the current maximum. a new value pops the candidates it beats, because they are smaller and older. so they cannot be the maximum of this window or a later one. an index that falls off the left of the window is popped from the front. longest unique substring length on abcabcbb returns 3. the window grows on the right and shrinks on the left whenever a repeated character enters. both ends move only forward. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: prefix sums
body: the idea a prefix sum array stores the total of every item up to each index. the library prefixsum on 1, 2, 3, 4 builds those totals once. range sum(start, end) returns the sum of values start:end , end exclusive. range sum(1, 3) is 2 + 3, which is 5. the formula is total end minus total start . the item at start is included and the item at end is not, matching a python slice. any later range on the same array is then a subtraction. counting subarrays that sum to a target uses the same totals. as you walk the array. a map from a previous prefix. to how many times it occurred tells you how many earlier starts would make the current prefix hit the target. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: backtracking search
body: the idea backtracking searches a tree of choices. you choose, recurse, and undo so the next choice sees the earlier state. permutations of 1, 2, 3 returns six lists, one for every order. the first position has three choices. the second has two remaining items. the third has one. the product is 6, and the function materializes each list. the undo step puts the chosen item back into the pool before the next sibling is tried. without the undo, the later branches would see a shrinking pool that is not restored. n queens count uses the same shape. a queen is placed, the search goes to the next row, and the placement is removed on the way back. pruning skips a placement that already shares a column or a diagonal with a queen. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: greedy methods
body: the idea a greedy algorithm makes a local choice and does not take it back. the choice needs an argument that some optimal solution agrees with it. interval scheduling max count on (1, 3, a), (2, 4, b), and (3, 5, c) returns 2. the rule sorts by finish time and takes the next interval that starts at or after the previous finish. a finishes first and is taken. b overlaps a and is skipped. c starts when a finishes and is taken. an example with three intervals does not prove the rule. the exchange argument does. huffman coding is another greedy choice. huffman codes on frequencies a 3, b 1, and c 1 gives a the code 1, the short code, because a is the frequent symbol. the two rare symbols share the longer branch. the library builds that tree by repeatedly combining the two lightest weights with a min-heap. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: dynamic programming state and transitions
body: the idea a dynamic-programming state is the smallest subproblem you are willing to store. the transition says how that state is computed from earlier states. for coin change, the state is the minimum number of coins that sum to an amount. min coin change on coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6 returns 2, for example 3 + 3. the transition tries each coin that does not exceed the amount and adds one to the answer for the remaining amount. amount 0 takes zero coins. a knapsack state needs two indexes. knapsack 01 on weights 1, 3, values 2, 4, and capacity 4 returns 6. both items fit, and their values sum to 6. the transition either skips the item or takes it when the remaining capacity allows. taking it is allowed once, which is why the item index moves forward. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: string search algorithms
body: the idea a naive search tries the pattern at every index of the text and compares characters until one differs. knuth-morris-pratt avoids restarting the text index after a partial match. kmp search of pattern ababa in text ababcababa returns 5. index 0 matches four characters and then fails, because the text has c where the pattern needs a. the failure links say how long a prefix of the pattern is also a suffix of the part just matched. so the search resumes in the middle of the pattern instead of at its first character. rabin karp search on the same strings also returns 5. it compares a rolling hash of the pattern with the hash of each window, and it still checks the characters when the hashes agree. a hash hit is a candidate, not a proof. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: tries and text indexes
body: the idea a trie stores strings along a path of characters. trie.insert walks or creates a child for each character. contains walks the same path and succeeds only when the whole key was inserted. after inserting cat and car, contains car is true, contains cat is true, and contains ca is false. ca is a prefix of both keys, and this trie does not treat a prefix as a stored key. a suffix array is a different index. suffix array with lcp on banana returns the suffix starts 5, 3, 1, 0, 4, 2 and an lcp array whose third entry is 3. the suffixes in that order are a, ana, anana, banana, na, nana. equal prefixes sit together, which is why a pattern query can binary-search the array. the lcp says how long the shared prefix of neighbors is, so you do not recompare those characters. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: range-query structures
body: the idea prefix sums answer a range in constant time until the array changes. a point update then costs a rebuild. a fenwick tree and a segment tree keep the update logarithmic. fenwicktree of length 4, after add 1 at index 0, add 2 at index 1. add 3 at index 2, reports prefix sum(2) equal to 6. the structure stores partial sums on ranges whose length is a power of two. a point add walks those ranges. a prefix query walks a different set and sums them. segmenttree on 1, 2, 3, 4 can add 5 to the inclusive span from index 1 to index 2. point query(1) becomes 7 and point query(0) stays 1. the lazy tag records the addition on a segment node and pushes it to children only when a later query needs them. sparsetable on 1, 3, 2, 4 answers range min(1, 3) with 2. the range is inclusive. the table does not support updates. it precomputes the minimum of every power-of-two span. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: approximate membership structures
body: the idea a bloom filter answers membership with a bit array and several hash functions. add sets the bits those hashes name. maybe contains returns true only when every one of those bits is set. bloomfilter with 64 bits, 3 hashes, and seed 0 inserts cat. maybe contains cat returns true. a false answer means the item was definitely never added, because add would have set those bits. a true answer means the item might have been added, or other items may have set the same bits. that is a false positive. which uninserted strings collide depends on the process hash salt, so this lesson does not pin a particular miss. this filter has no delete. clearing a bit could erase the evidence of a different item. the library states that contract on the class. a definite miss is the useful answer. it lets a storage engine skip a disk read. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: storage engines and locality
body: the idea storage engines place reads and writes in different structures. a b-tree keeps keys ordered in nodes with many children, so a lookup walks a short path. btree.insert of 2 and then 1 leaves search(1) true and search(9) false. the branching factor is the knob that trades taller trees for fatter nodes. a log-structured merge tree takes the other side of the trade. writes append to a memory table and a write-ahead log, then flush sorted runs. reads may check several runs. compaction merges those runs. the library's sequential scan sum of 1, 2, 3 returns 6. that scan touches neighboring items, which is the access pattern real disks and caches reward. a random jump to each key pays the same arithmetic and a worse memory pattern. locality is why the sum of a tight array is the baseline you compare against. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |

title: approximation guarantees
body: the idea some problems have no known exact algorithm that is fast on every input. an approximation algorithm returns a legal answer whose cost is provably close to the best cost. vertex cover two approximation scans edges and, when neither endpoint is already chosen, adds both. on a graph with only the edges a-b and c-d, the cover is the set a, b, c, d. the cover is feasible because every edge has both ends selected, so it certainly has one. an optimum cover can pick one end from each edge, so its size is 2. the algorithm returned 4, which is twice the optimum. the proof is the pairing. each time the algorithm adds two vertices, it does so for an edge whose ends were both still free. those edges do not share vertices. any cover must pick at least one vertex from each such edge. the algorithm picked two. the ratio is therefore at most 2 on every graph, not only on this one. a worked trace | step | state | what changed | |
